name: Cocos (Keeling) Islands
territory: Australia (external territory, administered by the Australian Government)

creatures.iucn_status: Endangered (EN), criteria A2bcd; assessment 17 July 2024 per FishBase (Wikipedia cites a 2004 assessment)
creatures.status_note: Presence verified via GBIF (24 Cocos records) and the Australian Faunal Directory; IUCN page itself could not be fetched, status relayed via FishBase/Wikipedia.

facts.statement: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands' capital, West Island, sits at roughly 12°11′13″ S, 96°49′42″ E in the eastern Indian Ocean.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox coordinates for West Island.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands lie about 3,685 km (2,290 mi) west of Darwin and about 900 km southwest of Christmas Island.
facts.evidence_note: Opening summary of the Britannica entry.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The group consists of 27 coral islands arranged in two atolls, and only West Island and Home Island have permanent residents.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section; SBS factbox also says 27 islands, 24 of them in South Keeling.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling, a small separate atoll, lies roughly 25 km north of the South Keeling atoll.
facts.evidence_note: Description of the two atolls in the image caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Cocos Island Airport, rainfall averages about 1,970 mm per year (records from 1901), peaking in April at about 243 mm and bottoming out in October at about 79 mm.
facts.source_title: Climate statistics for Cocos Island Airport (site 200284)
facts.evidence_note: Rainfall rows of the station averages table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Temperatures are steady: the mean daily maximum is about 29.1 °C and the mean minimum about 24.7 °C, with March warmest (mean max 30.1 °C) and July-August coolest (mean max 28.1 °C).
facts.source_title: Climate statistics for Cocos Island Airport (site 200284)
facts.evidence_note: Temperature rows of the station averages table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia classifies the climate as tropical rainforest (Köppen Af) with average annual rainfall of about 1,879 mm, wettest in April and driest in October.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section and climate chart data.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Australian government describes the climate as tropical and very humid, with temperatures of 23-30 °C, about 2,000 mm of rain a year mostly from January to August, and south-east trade winds most of the year.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A Ramsar site document notes Australia has warmed about 1.4 °C since 1910 and projects rising temperatures, falling rainfall and rising sea level for the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Climate change section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Total land area is only about 14.2 km2 with a 26 km coastline, and the highest point is about 5 m above sea level.
facts.evidence_note: Geography infobox figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The atolls are horseshoe-shaped, with coral-sand beaches on the ocean side and mudflats on the lagoon side.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Geography paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling is a C-shaped atoll of about 1.2 km2 enclosing a lagoon of about 0.5 km2, whose eastern opening is roughly 50 m wide.
facts.evidence_note: Description in the Area section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The low reef islands rise only 3-4 m above sea level and sit on a platform of cemented coral rock built from corals dated 4000-3000 radiocarbon years before present, with the islands accumulating over about the last 3000 years.
facts.source_title: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and what coral reefs can tell us about changes of sea level
facts.evidence_note: Cocos section of the sea-level vignette.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Charles Darwin visited in 1836 and developed his theory that atolls form as a sinking volcanic island leaves a coral ring behind; a NASA page says Beagle depth studies supported this idea.
facts.evidence_note: Geology paragraph; SERC page confirms 1836 visit and 1842 publication.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: William Keeling, a European captain, sighted the islands in 1609.
facts.evidence_note: History paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: John Clunies-Ross first visited in 1825 and later settled with his family, who ruled the islands almost like a private fiefdom for nearly 150 years.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: HMS Beagle reached the islands on 1 April 1836 with Charles Darwin aboard for survey work.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On 9 November 1914, HMAS Sydney fought the German raider SMS Emden off the islands, and the Emden ended up driven aground on North Keeling.
facts.evidence_note: Battle of Cocos entry; NAA page also says Emden was driven ashore on North Keeling.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands became an Australian territory on 23 November 1955 under the Cocos (Keeling) Islands Act 1955.
facts.evidence_note: Transfer paragraph; Australian government governance page gives the same date.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In a 1984 UN-supervised self-determination vote, 229 of 261 eligible voters chose full integration with Australia.
facts.evidence_note: History section vote tally; government page confirms the vote favoured integration.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands are an Australian external territory governed under section 122 of the Constitution, with a Minister for Territories, an Administrator appointed by the Governor-General, and Western Australian law applied through the 1955 Act.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Status and Act summary.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The population was 593 at the 2021 Census, mainly Cocos Malay people who mostly speak Malay at home (61.2%) and are mostly Sunni Muslims.
facts.evidence_note: Demographics section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Local services are run by the Shire of Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and residents vote federally in the Northern Territory Division of Lingiari.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Local government and electoral representation bullets.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling is the only seabird breeding area within 900 km, and about 60 bird species have been recorded across the islands.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Fauna section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling regularly supports about 30,000 breeding pairs of red-footed boobies, roughly 6% of the global population.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Species numbers in the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cocos buff-banded rail is the islands' only endemic bird; the Ramsar sheet estimates 422-711 birds on North Keeling and notes a 2013 reintroduction to Horsburgh Island.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Rail section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sixty-one plant species have been recorded in the territory, with one endemic subspecies, Pandanus tectorius cocosensis, found on Home and West Islands.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Flora section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The marine park region has over 600 reef fish species and a genetically distinct local green turtle stock.
facts.evidence_note: Species section of the marine park page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sea level is projected to rise about 14-17 cm by 2030 and 40-50 cm by 2070 at the national park, on islands only a few metres high.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park climate change strategy
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Sea level rise projections in the climate strategy.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone John in 1989 killed about 40% of booby chicks and 2% of adults, cut nest numbers by 60% the following year, and the colony recovered after four years.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park climate change strategy
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Red-footed booby passage in the strategy.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Yellow crazy ants were detected across 59 ha of North Keeling in 2009, and illegal seabird poaching was estimated at 2,000-3,000 birds a year in 2004.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Threats section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pulu Keeling National Park was established on 12 December 1995 and listed as Ramsar Site 797 on 17 March 1996, with legal hunting having ended in 1989.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation section; Ramsar site page confirms 17 March 1996 and 2,603 ha.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands Marine Park was proclaimed on 20 March 2022 and extends out to the edge of Australia's EEZ, covering roughly 467,000 km2.
facts.evidence_note: Establishment and size sections; page lists 467,054 and 467,754 km2.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: GBIF holds 24 occurrence records of Cheilinus undulatus from the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, including recent human observations.
facts.source_title: GBIF occurrence search: Cheilinus undulatus in Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.evidence_note: Occurrence search count and records.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: The Australian Faunal Directory lists the humphead (giant) wrasse as occurring at Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
facts.evidence_note: Distribution section citing Hobbs et al. 2014.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: FishBase reports the species as Endangered (criteria A2bcd) on the IUCN Red List, assessed 17 July 2024.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status line.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Wikipedia attributes the Endangered status to a 2004 IUCN assessment, which differs from the 2024 date shown by FishBase.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status citation.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Males can reach about 229 cm and 191 kg, while females rarely exceed 1 m.
facts.evidence_note: Description section; FishBase gives a similar 229 cm maximum.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: The species is a female-to-male sex changer that matures at 5-7 years and lives about 30 years.
facts.evidence_note: Biology section.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Its main threat is overfishing for the live reef food-fish trade, and it is listed in CITES Appendix II.
facts.evidence_note: Threats and CITES lines.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse
